COMPLETE REVIEW AND REVISION MEMO

Paper: “Is It the Game or the Agent? Measuring What a Game Hides, and Diagnosing Why an Agent Stops Improving”
Scope of this memo: technical review, conceptual positioning, experimental/design audit, writing review, likely reviewer objections, and prioritized revisions. This review is based on the supplied manuscript PDF and LaTeX source. It is intentionally candid and assumes the goal is to improve the paper before external review.

============================================================
1. EXECUTIVE ASSESSMENT
============================================================

This is a strong, unusually useful workshop paper with a memorable empirical message:

  (1) “Bits hidden” and “difficulty of learning” are different quantities.
  (2) A fixed-reference plateau cannot be interpreted without separating information limitation from learning limitation.
  (3) Common practical measurement machinery can fail silently in opposite directions.

The paper’s best contribution is not the 88-game atlas alone and not the Gin Rummy result alone. It is the combination of measurement provenance, a deliberately negative oracle-observation result, a matched placebo control, and small-game calibration. This makes the paper much more credible than a generic claim that “more hidden information does not necessarily mean harder RL.”

The central Gin Rummy result is especially provocative and potentially publishable as a methodological lesson: standard Gin Rummy has approximately 30.1 bits under the paper’s chosen information-set-cardinality definition, yet appending the opponent’s actual hand produces no detectable change in the trained learner’s win rate against the fixed expert: baseline 27.04%, oracle 26.79%, placebo 27.02%, with 12 seeds per arm. The control is well chosen: it rules out the explanation that a real benefit was cancelled by the cost of a wider input.

However, the paper currently overstates several conclusions and leaves its main estimand underspecified at exactly the place a careful reviewer will press hardest. The single most important revision is to distinguish, repeatedly and explicitly, among:

  A. information-set cardinality / log-cardinality,
  B. posterior Shannon entropy under a distribution over histories,
  C. hidden-hand combinatorial counts,
  D. decision-relevant value of information,
  E. what the particular learner captures under the training recipe.

At present, “bits of hidden information” is rhetorically clean but technically overloaded. The manuscript does acknowledge some of the issue, especially in its limitations and in the closed-form discussion, but it should make the distinction central rather than incidental. The paper’s most persuasive conclusion is not “Gin Rummy hides a lot but that information is useless.” It is narrower and better:

  Under the authors’ information-set-cardinality metric, standard Gin Rummy has a high amount of hidden-state ambiguity at sampled decision points; under this particular oracle-observation intervention, learner architecture/training recipe, fixed expert, and evaluation protocol, revealing the opponent hand did not yield a detectable win-rate improvement.

That conclusion is robust, interesting, and appropriately scoped.

Bottom-line recommendation: revise, strengthen definitions and claims, improve inferential discipline around the null, and add a small number of targeted diagnostics. Do not dilute the paper by adding many more games or models unless they directly resolve the paper’s key vulnerabilities.

============================================================
2. WHAT THE PAPER CONTRIBUTES
============================================================

The manuscript makes four interlocking contributions.

2.1 Atlas of hidden information

The paper defines hidden information at a decision as log2 of the number of histories consistent with the acting player’s information state and computes/report estimates over 88 game configurations from OpenSpiel and RLCard. It distinguishes exact enumeration, closed-form hand counts, and resampling. This is a valuable cataloguing/reproducibility contribution, especially because it reports method provenance rather than presenting a single false-precision table.

The empirical atlas claims are clear:

  - 2-player card games have median 3.1 measured bits.
  - Standard Gin Rummy is 30.1 bits, near the top of the 2-player-card range.
  - Higher values in many larger card games are associated with additional players/hands, not necessarily a deeper version of the same 2-player uncertainty problem.
  - Fog-of-war board games are a blind spot because no available estimator applies under the current setup.

2.2 Instrument-failure demonstration

This may be the most practically original portion of the paper. The resampling estimator has two failures:

  - Saturation: Hearts, Euchre, and contract bridge return exactly log2(80) = 6.32 bits because 80 samples are used and all samples are censored, whereas closed-form hand counts yield much larger values such as 56.2 for Hearts.
  - Degeneracy: all Gin Rummy variants return 0.00 bits with zero censoring because the engine resampler repeatedly returns the same world.

This is a compelling warning: simply sampling “possible worlds” and counting distinct samples cannot estimate a support larger than its sample budget, and a deterministic or faulty conditional-world generator can collapse a large information set to zero. The paper correctly argues that estimator provenance and cross-checks are essential.

2.3 Plateau-diagnosis probes

The paper offers three probes:

  - Capacity: vary encoders.
  - Value-of-information upper bound: compare fair determinized search and oracle search.
  - Oracle observation: append actual opponent cards to a learner’s observation, use a matched placebo plane, and compare results.

This is a coherent diagnostic framing, and the placebo is an excellent feature. The paper also checks that the extra information really reaches only the learner and verifies the custom oracle plane against engine state at 1,200 decision points.

2.4 Exact small-game decomposition

For solvable games, the paper defines “worth” as the oracle ceiling minus baseline ceiling and “capture” as learner gain divided by worth. It then studies how training budget affects capture but not exact worth. This is useful, particularly because the paper does not hide that capture is biased when the oracle and baseline arms differ in ease of optimization.

============================================================
3. GREEN FLAGS: WHAT IS WORKING VERY WELL
============================================================

3.1 The question is concrete and falsifiable

“Is the plateau caused by unavailable information or failure to learn from available information?” is a real research question, not just a benchmark report. The paper operationalizes it with interventions rather than relying on verbal explanations.

3.2 The paper has a genuine negative result, and it treats it better than most papers do

The Gin Rummy oracle result is not merely “not statistically significant.” The design includes:

  - 12 seeds per arm rather than the preliminary 4-seed result.
  - A reported mean difference and interval: -0.25 percentage points, 95% interval [-1.78, +1.28].
  - A same-shape, same-sparsity placebo channel.
  - Verification that the advertised oracle channel is actually the opponent hand, not PettingZoo’s larger “unknown cards” plane.
  - Cross-game evidence that the probe detects effects in small games where hidden state is useful.

That is unusually good experimental hygiene. The manuscript earns the right to say “no benefit detected,” although it should avoid stronger statements such as “changes nothing” without qualification.

3.3 The placebo design is thoughtful

The placebo is resampled once per deal rather than each decision, matching the temporal/input-distribution structure of the real oracle channel. The authors explicitly discovered and corrected a prior mismatch in pool size. Including this implementation history is a green flag because it tells reviewers that the authors thought through a subtle control rather than adding a superficial noise channel.

3.4 The paper distinguishes exact values from learned estimates

In the solvable games, the baseline and oracle ceilings are exact values under the stated policy/game formulation. The paper does not incorrectly attach seed uncertainty to those values. It correctly places seed noise on learner performance instead.

3.5 It openly documents limitations and failures

The manuscript acknowledges:

  - Strategy-fusion confounding in determinized search.
  - Closed-form overcounting due to ignored public information.
  - The fact that small exactly solvable games differ from Gin Rummy.
  - Biased capture ratios.
  - The limited architecture sweep.
  - Unmeasured fog-of-war games.

This intellectual honesty is a major strength and likely to play well in an evaluation-oriented workshop.

3.6 The central empirical contrast is memorable

Gin Rummy at 30.1 bits produces no detectable learned oracle benefit; poker and Liar’s Dice variants at roughly 1–4 bits do. That is exactly the kind of result that forces a conceptual distinction between uncertainty quantity and uncertainty value.

3.7 The manuscript has a good narrative spine

The current story is logically ordered:

  - We do not measure what games hide.
  - Our measurement tool itself can lie.
  - A game’s hiddenness does not diagnose an agent’s plateau.
  - Here are interventions that diagnose the plateau.

This is much stronger than a “we measured 88 games” paper alone.

============================================================
4. RED FLAGS AND HIGH-PRIORITY TECHNICAL ISSUES
============================================================

4.1 The core metric is not fully pinned down

This is the largest issue.

The paper defines hidden information as:

  log2(number of histories consistent with the acting player’s information state).

That is log-cardinality of an information set. But the paper then uses language such as “bits of hidden information,” “worlds the player must consider,” “how much the player cannot see,” and “Gin Rummy hides 30.1 bits.” Those phrases invite readers to interpret the metric as Shannon conditional entropy. It is not generally Shannon entropy unless all compatible histories are equally probable conditional on the information state.

Why this matters:

  - A player’s actual belief state is generally nonuniform because chance, public actions, and policy-induced selection alter posterior probabilities.
  - In Gin Rummy, public draw/pass/discard behavior can make compatible opponent hands very nonuniformly likely.
  - The value of revealing a hidden hand depends on payoff-relevant posterior structure, not raw support size.
  - A log-cardinality measure can be large even when posterior entropy is small; conversely, posterior entropy and support can differ dramatically in stochastic games with unequal history probabilities.

Required fix:

Add a formal boxed definition early in Section 2. Use a term that cannot be mistaken for entropy, for example:

  “information-set log-cardinality,”
  “possible-world ambiguity,” or
  “support bits.”

Then write explicitly:

  “This is not posterior Shannon entropy. It ignores probability weights over histories and should not be read as an estimate of a player’s subjective uncertainty or the value of observing the state.”

Also add a short relation table:

  Quantity: information-set log-cardinality. Formula: log2 |I(o)|. Interpretation: number of compatible histories under the game model.
  Quantity: posterior entropy. Formula: H(S|O=o). Interpretation: uncertainty under a specified distribution/policy.
  Quantity: decision value of information. Formula: V*(O,S) - V*(O). Interpretation: payoff value of revealing state.
  Quantity: learned oracle gap. Formula: learner_oracle - learner_baseline. Interpretation: what this learner/training setup uses.

This single clarification would strengthen the paper substantially.

4.2 “At a typical decision” requires a sampling-distribution definition

The phrase “at a typical decision” appears repeatedly. It is a major source of ambiguity.

Typical under what distribution?

  - Uniform over histories?
  - Uniform over legal decision nodes?
  - Uniform over turns/plies?
  - On-policy distribution under random play, self-play, a fixed heuristic, or an equilibrium policy?
  - Weighted by visit probability under chance and a behavior policy?
  - Player-to-move states only, pooled across players or separately?
  - Conditional on nonterminal states?

For log-cardinality, the average of log2|I(o)| depends heavily on how decision states are weighted. This can alter cross-game comparisons. A game may have rare, enormous information sets but low average ambiguity under natural play; another may have moderate ambiguity at nearly every decision.

Required fix:

State the exact state-sampling protocol in the main paper, not only code. Give notation. For example:

  “For each game, we sample N decision states by [procedure], condition on [conditions], compute b(o)=log2|I(o)|, and report [mean/median]. The number is therefore an on-policy/trajectory-weighted average over the specified distribution, not a property of the rules alone independent of a state distribution.”

If currently reporting a mean, say so. If reporting a median, say so. If the 30.1 figure is a closed-form static configuration-level count rather than a time-average, do not call it “at a typical decision” without a clear bridge.

Recommended addition:

Show a distribution or at least quantiles for Gin Rummy across decisions: e.g., 10th/50th/90th percentile ambiguity, or an ambiguity-vs-turn/stock-size plot. This would directly answer the obvious question: does 30.1 remain stable during play, and why?

4.3 The Gin Rummy 30.1-bit number needs a sharper explanation

A technically sophisticated reviewer may immediately calculate a standard opening-hand count and get a number near 31 bits for the opponent’s 10-card hand from 41 unknown cards. They may then expect the count to decline as public discards accumulate. If your reported “typical decision” figure is still 30.1 bits, the paper must explain exactly why.

Possible reasons could include:

  - The count is a full history count, retaining hidden stock order and hidden private history rather than only the current opponent hand.
  - The number is tied to a particular state distribution dominated by early states.
  - The closed form is not conditioning on public card eliminations and thus acts as a coarse upper count.
  - The observation model does not retain/publicly distinguish certain events.

Whatever the actual reason, state it plainly. Right now the reader has to infer too much.

Required fix:

Add a Gin Rummy worked example in the main paper or appendix:

  - State what is observed at an example decision.
  - State precisely what the latent world includes.
  - Count or illustrate the compatible histories.
  - Explain what information the 30.1-bit figure includes and excludes.
  - Contrast it with the smaller “current opponent hand only” count after public cards are removed.

This will prevent the paper from appearing to exploit a large number that is semantically different from what readers intuitively mean by “the opponent’s hidden hand.”

4.4 Closed form is described as “exact arithmetic” but is not an exact estimate of the stated target

The paper says closed form “is exact arithmetic but counts hands only, ignoring what public cards have ruled out, so it overestimates mildly.” This is mathematically fine but rhetorically risky. It is exact arithmetic for a surrogate count, not exact for the information-set log-cardinality definition in the previous sentence.

The paper needs terminology like:

  - “exact combinatorial proxy,” not merely “closed form.”
  - “exact for the specified hand-deal model, approximate/upper bounding for information-set cardinality.”

Also, “overestimates mildly” is shown only for Leduc’s 2.30 versus 2.01 comparison. It may not be mild in all games. Public observations may rule out a substantial fraction of deals in games with rich public action histories. The evidence does not support a general “mildly” claim unless you have a broader exact-vs-closed-form calibration table.

Required fix:

Replace “overestimates mildly” with “can overestimate; in the Leduc calibration it is 2.30 versus 2.01 bits.” If you have more exact rows, report error ranges and relative error across all rows with both methods. That would be much stronger.

4.5 Resampling section should distinguish an estimator failure from an implementation failure

The current section says “resampling fails silently in both directions.” The saturation result is a general limitation of the proposed distinct-sample-count estimator. The Gin Rummy zero result, however, seems to be a resampler/engine degeneracy: the engine hands back the same world every draw.

These are not exactly the same kind of failure:

  - Saturation: an unavoidable upper bound of a finite-sample observed-distinct-count procedure without structural extrapolation; at most log2(n) bits can be demonstrated by n distinct samples.
  - Degeneracy: a correctness/implementation/semantics failure in the conditional-world generator; repeated world draws do not establish that the support is size 1.

Calling both “resampling estimator” failures is defensible as a practical warning, but a reviewer may say the second is merely a bug in a library function and does not indict resampling itself.

Required fix:

Make the distinction explicit. Suggested framing:

  “We find two operational failure modes of a sampling-based measurement pipeline: sample-budget saturation, which is intrinsic to support counting, and generator degeneracy, which is an implementation/semantics failure. Both can yield plausible scalar outputs without an internal alarm.”

This is more precise and harder to dismiss.

4.6 The saturation result needs a formal censoring protocol and a non-identifiability statement

The paper says samples are “censored at the sample count” and labels the graph “hatched: resampled floor.” But a number equal to log2(80) should not be interpreted as an estimate at all; it is a lower bound on support log-cardinality conditional on successful distinct sampling, or simply a right-censored observation.

Required fixes:

  - Mark all saturation results as “>= log2(n)” or “right-censored at log2(n),” not as point estimates in plots/tables.
  - State whether repeated samples can occur legitimately and how “censored” is detected.
  - Explain why no confidence interval or extrapolated estimate is reported.
  - Explicitly say that distinct-count resampling cannot distinguish, for example, 2^10, 2^30, and 2^100 support if samples are overwhelmingly unique at the available budget.

This turns a good empirical observation into a rigorous methodological point.

4.7 The central conclusion “learning-bound” is too strong from the current evidence

The paper concludes: “this agent is learning-bound, in a game that genuinely hides a great deal” and “effort belongs in optimisation, reward and curriculum, not in belief modelling.” This is the biggest overclaim in the narrative.

What the Gin Rummy experiment shows:

  - Giving one learner/recipe the opponent’s current hand as an extra plane did not produce a detectable performance change against one fixed rule-based expert under a particular training and evaluation protocol.
  - This does not prove that all belief modeling is unhelpful.
  - It does not prove that hidden information has low normative value against stronger/adaptive opponents or under self-play/equilibrium evaluation.
  - It does not prove that the learner’s plateau is purely optimization/reward/curriculum limited; the oracle channel may be difficult to use in the current architecture, loss, credit assignment, or data regime even if a more structured belief representation would help.
  - It does not identify whether the hidden information is truly low value versus the learner failing to exploit raw oracle information.

The authors themselves acknowledge that capacity sweeps are limited and that oracle access changes learning difficulty. The conclusion should match that caution.

Recommended revision:

Replace “learning-bound” with:

  “not shown to be information-bound under this oracle-observation intervention,”
  “the hidden-hand oracle does not explain the observed plateau against this fixed expert,” or
  “the observed plateau is not relieved by direct access to the opponent hand under the evaluated recipe.”

Replace “effort belongs in optimisation, reward and curriculum, not in belief modelling” with:

  “The present evidence prioritizes testing optimization, reward, curriculum, and representation/credit-assignment hypotheses before attributing the plateau to lack of opponent-hand observability. It does not rule out benefits from structured belief modeling under other opponents or objectives.”

This narrower conclusion is still strong and more defensible.

4.8 A confidence interval containing zero is not evidence of no useful effect

The manuscript generally uses “no benefit detected,” which is good. But the title/captions/phrasing sometimes slide toward “the hidden hand changes nothing.” With 12 seeds and interval [-1.78, +1.28] percentage points, the experiment excludes only effects larger than approximately +1.28 pp at the chosen confidence convention. It leaves open smaller benefits.

Required fix:

Define a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) or practical equivalence margin before/alongside the analysis. For example, if 1 pp is practically meaningful, the current CI almost but not entirely supports ruling out effects above 1 pp; if 0.5 pp is meaningful, it does not. Better yet, run an equivalence test or report a confidence interval for the oracle-minus-placebo contrast as well.

Key contrasts to report:

  - Oracle - baseline: -0.25 pp.
  - Placebo - baseline: -0.03 pp.
  - Oracle - placebo: -0.23 pp.

The oracle-versus-placebo contrast is the direct estimate of the incremental value of meaningful content after controlling for width/shape. It should be in the main figure/table, with an interval.

4.9 Independence and effective sample size are unclear

The paper reports 12 seeds per arm and evaluates 600 games per seed. The unit of variation is presumably training seed, which is correct if each seed has an aggregate evaluation score. But reviewers will ask:

  - Are evaluation match seeds shared across agents/arms (paired evaluation), or independently sampled?
  - Are the same training environments/curriculum schedules used across corresponding seeds?
  - Does each seed’s 600-game evaluation have binomial/match-level uncertainty that is negligible relative to between-seed variance?
  - How was the reported 95% interval for the difference computed: independent two-sample t, paired t, bootstrap over seeds, or a hierarchical model?
  - Were seeds paired across arms? If so, using a paired analysis could sharply improve power.

Required fix:

Add one paragraph with the full inferential unit and method. Prefer reporting seed-level dots and a paired design if it existed. If training seeds cannot be paired in a meaningful way, state that arms are independent and use Welch intervals/tests. If all evaluation game seeds were shared, say so.

4.10 The fixed expert matters more than the paper currently conveys

The paper makes a subset argument: the expert observes a strict subset of learner information and scores roughly 50% against itself, so parity is achievable from the learner’s observation. This is useful, but it does not explain why revealing the expert’s actual hand is not valuable below parity.

A hidden hand may have negligible value against a particular deterministic rule-based expert because:

  - The expert may make locally predictable choices that public history already reveals.
  - The learner might not be in a position to exploit hand-specific weaknesses with its action set.
  - The expert may be weak for reasons unrelated to hidden state.
  - The evaluation score could be driven by learner self-hand quality and generic tactical play rather than opponent-conditioned defense.

The current conclusions need explicit “against this fixed expert” qualifiers in every major takeaway. A stronger test, if feasible, would compare oracle effects against more than one frozen reference: a random but nontrivial policy, a different heuristic family, a stronger search policy, and perhaps a curriculum/opponent population. This would establish whether the null is an interaction with the specific expert.

4.11 “Value of information” search result is not an upper bound in the clean decision-theoretic sense

The paper calls fair versus oracle determinized search a “value of information, as an upper bound,” then acknowledges strategy fusion. This is close but potentially misleading.

Because determinization with oracle access changes not only information but also the search representation and strategy-fusion pathology, the gap is not a clean upper bound on the normative value of state revelation. Depending on setup, strategy fusion can affect fair search in ways that make the gap larger or otherwise distorted. The paper says this but then still relies on “bounds what the hidden information is worth.”

Required fix:

Call it an “oracle-search gap” or “search-based diagnostic upper proxy,” not “value of information” without a modifier. Say:

  “It upper-bounds the benefit within this determinized-search protocol only; it is not an identified decision-theoretic value of information because oracle access also changes strategy fusion and planning error.”

If you can calculate a clean exact value in smaller games, use those results to define “worth” and reserve that term for the exact setting. Do not reuse it for Gin Rummy unless you make the qualification prominent.

4.12 The capacity probe does not isolate capacity cleanly

The paper calls the encoder comparison a capacity probe. But switching MLP to self-attention changes inductive bias, optimization, compute, hyperparameters, possibly regularization and training dynamics; it is not a monotonic capacity sweep. The results show “these two tested encoder families did not improve the result under this recipe,” not “network capacity is not the limit.”

The appendix’s bucket sweep is a more direct capacity intervention for small games. In Gin Rummy, the paper could describe the MLP/attention comparison as an “architecture sensitivity check” rather than an adequate capacity diagnosis.

Recommended revision:

  - Rename main probe 1 to “architecture sensitivity” unless you actually vary parameter count/representation capacity while matching optimization and compute.
  - Soften verdict from “no” to “no improvement among tested encoders.”
  - If possible, add width/depth/parameter-count scaling with sufficiently controlled training budgets.

4.13 The phrase “A 52-card deck split between two hands cannot conceal much more” is vague and potentially false under your stated metric

If the metric counts complete histories, stock order and private draw history can add very large ambiguity beyond the opponent’s unordered hand. The sentence seems to mean “under the hand-only closed form used here,” but it reads as a general claim about Gin-like card games.

Required fix:

Qualify the statement:

  “Under our hand-only closed-form proxy with the specified deal sizes, a 52-card two-player deal has a limited maximum range.”

Or remove it unless you prove an explicit bound under the exact metric.

4.14 “More hidden information means more players” is causal/rhetorical overreach

The atlas shows that the 3–4 player family has higher measured ambiguity, and additional opponent hands mechanically add combinatorial allocations. But “more hidden information means more players” is a slogan that invites counterexamples: one can add private state, hidden board, stochasticity, or sequential secret information without more players. The manuscript later says extra bits are “bought with extra hands,” which is more precise.

Recommended revision:

Use “In this atlas, higher card-game counts are primarily driven by additional players’ hands” rather than a general statement.

4.15 The 88-game atlas is heterogeneous in a way that needs more methodological accounting

Games differ by:

  - source engine,
  - information-state encoding conventions,
  - action history observability,
  - chance model,
  - repeated or identical physical cards,
  - player count,
  - selected game parameters,
  - state-sampling regime,
  - whether measurement is exact, proxy, censored, or failed.

The paper acknowledges methods but Figure 1 still visually encourages a precise cross-game ranking. The plot should more aggressively encode comparability/provenance. One visible label “hatched: resampled floor” is likely insufficient.

Required fixes:

  - Include estimator type beside every point/bar or facet the plot by estimator class.
  - Use a distinct visual treatment for exact, combinatorial proxy, right-censored lower bound, and unavailable.
  - Provide a machine-readable table in supplement/repository with game parameters, source, sampling distribution, method, sample budget, censoring percentage, and notes.
  - Avoid ranking prose based on values that mix exact information-set counts and hand-only proxies without caveat.

4.16 Exact enumeration is ground truth only relative to game implementation and information-state representation

“Exact enumeration walks the tree and groups histories by information state. This is ground truth” is a little too absolute. It is ground truth for the specified extensive-form game as implemented and the engine’s observation/information-state function. An engine may encode private or public history differently from what a human player sees, and perfect recall assumptions matter.

Recommended revision:

“Exact enumeration is ground truth for the implemented game and its declared information-state representation.”

This is a minor wording change with major methodological maturity.

4.17 The paper should discuss history identity versus strategically distinct hidden states

Counting histories means that two hidden worlds that induce the same current state, same future transition law, and same continuation values may still count separately because their past differs. That can inflate “bits” without increasing the complexity of decision making. This may be especially relevant for Gin Rummy if hidden stock order/private draw histories are counted.

This is conceptually central to the paper’s result. The paper needs a paragraph distinguishing:

  - history-level ambiguity,
  - current latent-state ambiguity,
  - strategically relevant state abstraction / value-equivalence classes.

A strong way to formulate this:

  “Our atlas deliberately measures observation-consistent histories, not minimal sufficient state for control. Thus it is a measure of observational ambiguity, not a minimal decision-state complexity. The Gin Rummy oracle result shows why this distinction matters.”

That would make the apparent “30 bits yet no gain” result a conceptual feature rather than a confusion to defend against.

============================================================
5. CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK THE PAPER SHOULD ADOPT
============================================================

The paper will become much clearer if it explicitly presents a four-layer hierarchy.

Layer 1: Observable ambiguity

For player observation o, let I(o) be the set of complete histories compatible with o.

  B_support(o) = log2 |I(o)|.

This is the paper’s primary atlas number. It measures support size, not likelihood weighting and not decision value.

Layer 2: Belief uncertainty

Given a distribution over histories, induced by chance and a policy profile pi:

  B_entropy(o; pi) = H(HiddenState | O=o; pi).

This measures posterior uncertainty. It depends on policy and state distribution. It can be lower than support bits if actions make some histories much more probable than others.

Layer 3: Normative value of information

Let Z be the hidden variable revealed by an oracle and O be the ordinary observation. Against a fixed opponent policy, define:

  VOI(o) = E_Z[ max_a Q*(o, Z, a) ] - max_a E_Z[ Q*(o, Z, a) ].

Averaging this over the state distribution yields the expected value of revealing Z. This is the right object for “is opponent-hand information useful?” It may be zero even when B_support is large.

Layer 4: Learned use of information

For learning procedure L, architecture A, budget T, and evaluation setup E:

  OracleGap_L = Performance(L with O,Z) - Performance(L with O).

This is an intervention-dependent empirical quantity. It conflates available value, representation, optimization, training data, credit assignment, and generalization. The placebo measures a particular nuisance component: widening/input-format cost.

Suggested core thesis after revision:

  “Information-set log-cardinality quantifies observational ambiguity; exact value-of-information quantifies what revelation could improve; and an oracle-observation learner quantifies what a particular training procedure actually captures. The three can diverge sharply.”

This formulation makes the paper more rigorous and protects it from the obvious critique that 30 bits “should” imply value.

============================================================
6. INTERPRETING THE GIN RUMMY RESULT CORRECTLY
============================================================

The manuscript’s empirical result is highly interesting, but it should be interpreted as a dissociation, not a contradiction.

6.1 Why 30 support bits can coexist with zero observable oracle gain

Many distinct hidden histories may produce the same action ranking. Suppose the learner is choosing a discard. Exact knowledge of the opponent hand matters only when it changes which discard is optimal, and changes it by enough expected value, frequently enough, to affect aggregate win rate.

Formally, let a*(o) be the best action under ordinary observation and a*(o,z) be the best action under the oracle state. Oracle information has local decision value only when:

  a*(o,z) != a*(o)

and when the regret of using a*(o) in state z is material. Large |I(o)| does not guarantee either condition.

In Gin Rummy, several mechanisms can make hidden-hand support large but action value small:

  - The player’s own hand and public card structure may dominate discard/draw/knock decisions.
  - Many opponent hands may be equivalent with respect to whether a candidate card is dangerous.
  - Public draws, passes, and discards may already reveal the salient opponent-meld features even though they leave many exact card identities unknown.
  - The fixed rule-based expert may be exploitable through policy regularities unrelated to its exact current hand.
  - The game’s value may be spread across many small, noisy decisions; a local oracle advantage may not move the coarse match win rate much.
  - The raw hand plane may be a poor inductive-bias format for the policy to convert into counterfactual action values.

6.2 What the current test can and cannot conclude

It can conclude:

  - Under the tested recipe and fixed-expert evaluation, raw exact opponent-hand input does not yield a detectable win-rate benefit of more than approximately the upper interval bound.
  - The result is not explained by a simple input-widening penalty, given the matched placebo’s near-zero difference.
  - The experimental apparatus can detect effects in several small control games.

It cannot conclude:

  - Opponent-hand information has zero normative value in Gin Rummy.
  - Belief modeling is generally unhelpful in Gin Rummy.
  - No representation of opponent state can help.
  - The agent is fully “learning-bound” rather than information-bound in all meaningful senses.
  - The result generalizes to self-play, equilibrium play, stronger experts, different action abstractions, alternative reward functions, or longer training.

6.3 Strong targeted analyses to add

If you can add only one new diagnostic, add an oracle-action-sensitivity analysis.

At held-out decision states, compare oracle-conditioned and non-oracle decisions or action values. Estimate:

  - Frequency of action changes when the hidden hand is revealed.
  - Conditional on action change, estimated action-value margin/regret.
  - Breakdown by decision type: draw, discard, knock.
  - Breakdown by phase: early/mid/late or stock size.

Even if the trained policies are imperfect, this analysis can show whether the oracle plane is being used at all and whether potential effect is concentrated in rare states.

If you can add two diagnostics, add oracle-derived structured features:

  - For each candidate discard, whether the opponent can immediately use it in a meld.
  - Opponent’s deadwood after receiving each candidate card.
  - Whether opponent is one card from gin/knock.
  - Opponent’s best immediate meld/deadwood score.

Interpretation:

  - If structured privileged features help but raw hand does not, the null is likely representation/learning/credit assignment rather than absent value.
  - If neither helps, the case for low usable value against this expert becomes substantially stronger.

If you can add a third diagnostic, use counterfactual rollouts or a restricted planner to estimate a decision-level oracle advantage under matched compute. This would separate “the agent cannot learn the implication” from “the hidden hand rarely changes an advantageous response.”

============================================================
7. EXPERIMENTAL AND STATISTICAL REVIEW
============================================================

7.1 Gin Rummy arm statistics

Current reported values:

  Baseline: n=12, mean 27.04, SD 1.87, 95% CI [25.86, 28.23].
  Oracle: n=12, mean 26.79, SD 1.52, 95% CI [25.82, 27.76].
  Placebo: n=12, mean 27.02, SD 1.65, 95% CI [25.97, 28.06].

These intervals are group-mean intervals, not necessarily intervals for the differences. The main text gives an interval for oracle minus baseline, but it should provide all planned contrasts and specify construction.

Recommended reporting table:

  Contrast                 Estimate (pp)    95% CI    Interpretation
  Oracle - baseline        -0.25            [...]      content + any residual format effect
  Placebo - baseline       -0.03            [...]      widening/format effect
  Oracle - placebo         -0.23            [...]      information-content effect net of placebo

Also report standardized effect sizes with uncertainty, but do not substitute standardization for raw units.

7.2 Practical-equivalence analysis

The manuscript should decide what effect size is worth caring about. If +1 pp is the smallest practically meaningful improvement against the expert, make that explicit. Then perform a two one-sided tests (TOST) equivalence analysis or frame the CI relative to the equivalence margin.

Example language, if justified:

  “With a pre-specified practical margin of ±1 percentage point, the 95% confidence interval for oracle-minus-baseline [x,y] [does/does not] establish practical equivalence.”

Do not choose the margin after seeing the result without saying so.

7.3 Multiple comparisons and exploratory claims

The paper reports a broad atlas, multiple game families, multiple methods, several probes, and correlations. It need not mechanically correct every descriptive comparison, but it should label which claims are confirmatory versus exploratory. The “perfect rank correlation” result across 11 related configurations is visually compelling but should not be overread as a strong p-value-based confirmation because configurations are not independent.

The manuscript already acknowledges dependence. A more reviewer-proof version would remove or de-emphasize the p=9 x 10^-8 line; it looks statistically stronger than the design supports. The within-family rank ordering is the more relevant qualitative evidence.

7.4 Evaluation opponent and metric sensitivity

The paper should ideally assess whether the oracle null persists under:

  - At least one additional fixed opponent.
  - A stronger opponent or a policy derived from different heuristics/search.
  - A return/score margin metric rather than only match win rate.
  - Possibly a “win probability over game stages” or per-hand score metric.

Win rate is a valid ultimate metric but potentially insensitive. Oracle knowledge could reduce deadwood or prevent opponent gin events without moving enough match wins in 600-game evaluations.

7.5 Training-budget sensitivity for Gin Rummy

You show learning-budget behavior for solvable games but not for Gin Rummy. A reviewer will ask whether oracle benefit emerges only at longer training horizons. If a full sweep is costly, provide at least two or three budget points for Gin Rummy or state why not. This is more valuable than adding further atlas rows.

7.6 Check for leakage and causal matching

The manuscript is good here, but tighten the description:

  - Confirm that oracle input is available at exactly the same temporal point as each decision and uses no post-action information.
  - Confirm that the oracle does not alter environment state, opponent observation, legal action mask, reward, reset logic, or curriculum selection.
  - Confirm the placebo distribution matches not only cardinality and sparsity but also per-card marginal frequencies, temporal stability, and canonical ordering/encoding.
  - State whether the oracle cards are sorted/canonicalized; if so, the placebo should use the same canonicalization to avoid an unintended feature-complexity difference.

7.7 Probe validation controls

The controls are good but the language “it detects the hidden state everywhere it is present” is too broad. It detects a positive effect in the selected small games and configurations, not all possible settings where information is present. Change to:

  “In the tested solvable benchmark configurations, the same intervention yields positive effects while the placebo remains near baseline.”

============================================================
8. WRITING AND PRESENTATION ISSUES
============================================================

8.1 Strengths of the writing

The prose is compact, confident, and readable. Headings such as “When the instrument lies” are memorable. The paper has a clear thesis and avoids generic related-work padding. The authors explain their controls rather than only listing them. The use of exact numbers in the abstract is effective.

8.2 Main writing risk: rhetoric outruns the estimand

Several phrases are strong enough to invite technical attack:

  - “Two measurements nobody makes.”
  - “How much the player to move cannot see.”
  - “More hidden information means more players.”
  - “A 52-card deck split between two hands cannot conceal much more.”
  - “the hidden hand changes nothing.”
  - “the probe fires wherever the information is there.”
  - “this agent is learning-bound.”
  - “effort belongs in optimisation, reward and curriculum, not in belief modelling.”

These phrases are useful as hooks but should be softened or qualified immediately in nearby text. The paper will be stronger if it sounds precise rather than categorical.

8.3 Title and terminology

The title is good. Consider changing the subtitle or opening definition to use “observational ambiguity” or “information-set ambiguity” so reviewers do not assume Shannon entropy. Examples:

  “Measuring Observational Ambiguity in Games, and Diagnosing Why an Agent Stops Improving.”

or retain the title but add a subtitle clause:

  “Measuring Information-Set Ambiguity and Diagnosing Why an Agent Stops Improving.”

If you retain “what a game hides,” define it as a specific operational measure in the first paragraph.

8.4 Abstract revisions

The abstract is energetic but overly dense. It mixes three major results, several numbers, and multiple claims. Most important changes:

  - State “information-set log-cardinality” rather than “bits of hidden information.”
  - Say “under the stated state-sampling distribution.”
  - Describe resampling outputs as “right-censored at the sample budget” and “degenerate due to repeated world output,” if space permits.
  - Replace “they agree” regarding probes: the probes do not fully agree in the sense that oracle search has a large gap while oracle learner has none; rather, they jointly show different parts of the diagnostic.
  - Replace “learning-bound” conclusion with the narrower causal claim.

8.5 Section 1 needs citations/related-work positioning

“Two measurements nobody makes” is too broad without careful literature support. There is extensive work on information sets, state-space complexity, entropy/mutual information, value of information, partial observability, belief-state RL, and benchmark diagnostics. The novelty is likely not that nobody has ever measured these concepts, but that this paper combines a cross-game empirical atlas, provenance-aware estimators, and oracle/placebo diagnostics for a plateau.

Add a short related-work paragraph or a dedicated Related Work section addressing:

  - Information-set and game-tree complexity in extensive-form games.
  - Entropy / partial observability metrics and POMDP belief-state literature.
  - Oracle/privileged-information studies, e.g. learning with privileged information and state-augmentation ablations in RL.
  - Imperfect-information game benchmarks and search pathologies/strategy fusion.
  - RL evaluation reliability, seed variation, and fixed-baseline evaluation.

Do not frame the paper as if all predecessor work is absent. Frame it as a missing integrated measurement-and-diagnosis workflow.

8.6 Clarify “expert” versus “reference” versus “opponent policy”

The deterministic rule-based player is called an “expert.” If it is not demonstrably expert-level, reviewers may object. “Fixed rule-based reference policy” is safer and more neutral. If the source paper calls it expert, retain the term with qualifications but use “fixed reference” in methodological claims.

8.7 Fix terminology consistency

The paper alternates among:

  - hidden state,
  - hidden information,
  - hidden cards,
  - opponent hand,
  - worlds,
  - histories,
  - information state,
  - oracle state.

These are not all the same. Establish notation and use it consistently:

  h = full history;
  s = latent current state;
  o = player information state/observation;
  z = oracle-revealed variable (opponent hand);
  I(o) = compatible histories.

Then be deliberate about whether each result is about h, s, or z.

8.8 Figure and table issues

Figure 1:

  - It communicates the headline well but mixes exact, proxy, censored, and possibly unavailable results. Add estimator markers or split panels.
  - The main visual claim that 2p games “saturate” risks conflating a genuine distributional pattern with tool limitations and the selected benchmark set.
  - “Hatched: resampled floor” should instead say “right-censored lower bound at log2(80)” if that is what it means.

Figure 2:

  - Good seed-level visualization.
  - Add the oracle-minus-placebo contrast in caption or adjacent text.
  - The title “the hidden hand changes nothing” should be changed to “No detectable benefit from the hidden-hand channel under this evaluation” or similarly precise wording.

Figure 3:

  - Standardizing by “seed spread” needs a precise formula. Is it pooled SD? Baseline SD? SD of paired differences? This must be stated.
  - The log x-axis including negative values is visually/non-mathematically awkward. A log scale cannot directly show negative effects. The displayed ticks “-1, 0, 1, 10, 100” require explanation; likely this is a transformed/symlog scale. Label the transform.
  - The phrase “everywhere it is present” is too categorical.

Table 2:

  - “Value of information” should be renamed “oracle-search gap (confounded upper proxy).”
  - “Capacity” verdict “no” should be softened.
  - The reported oracle-observation values “24.7 vs 25.5 baseline” conflict with the 27.04/26.79 numbers in Figure 2 and Table 8. This looks like a serious inconsistency. It may reflect outdated numbers, a different configuration, or a table-generation error. Resolve before submission. This is exactly the kind of issue a reviewer will flag as evidence that tables are not synchronized.

This Table 2 discrepancy is a top-priority red flag. The manuscript text elsewhere reports 27.04 baseline and 26.79 oracle. Table 2 says 24.7 vs 25.5 baseline. Determine which is correct, regenerate all artifacts, and make sure the PDF is rebuilt from current data.

Table 3:

  - Clarify return scale across games; “worth” values are not comparable to Gin Rummy win-rate percentage points.
  - “Capture” needs an explicit formula in the caption or immediately preceding text.
  - Do not imply that capture is a clean learner property given the documented differential optimization-gap bias.

8.9 Appendix language needs restraint

“The workshop does not require reviewers to read an appendix, so nothing here is load bearing” is understandable but a little adversarial/defensive. It may irritate reviewers. Better:

  “The main text contains the primary claims and results; the appendix provides implementation details, full tables, and additional robustness analyses.”

Similarly, internal comments about submission mechanics are fine in source but should be checked carefully not to appear in released artifacts or source distributions if anonymity policy matters.

============================================================
9. SPECIFIC INCONSISTENCIES OR ITEMS TO VERIFY
============================================================

9.1 Table 2 numerical mismatch

As noted above, Table 2 says oracle observation: “24.7 vs 25.5 baseline,” while Figure 2, main text, abstract, and Table 8 say 26.79 oracle versus 27.04 baseline. This must be fixed.

9.2 “12 seeds each side” wording

Use “12 independent training seeds per arm,” not “each side,” which is ambiguous in a three-arm design.

9.3 Meaning of 30.1 bits

Verify whether the 30.1 is:

  - a mean of log-cardinality across sampled decision states,
  - a single opening/initial-state combinatorial count,
  - a hand-only closed form,
  - a full-history count,
  - a median, or
  - something else.

The manuscript must say so unambiguously. This is foundational.

9.4 Exact enumeration count of 11 rows

List the 11 rows or provide them in a supplement table. Readers will want to know which games have ground truth, exact state-space sizes, and whether they span enough structure to validate closed forms/resampling.

9.5 Use of “CFR supplies a true optimum”

CFR asymptotically approaches equilibrium in the relevant class; it does not automatically “supply a true optimum” merely because a game is small. If you use a solved/verified CFR convergence criterion or exact dynamic program, say so. Otherwise phrase more carefully:

  “small enough to solve to numerical tolerance with CFR” or “for which we compute/verify an equilibrium benchmark.”

Also be precise about whether the oracle comparison is to a best response against a fixed opponent, an equilibrium value, or a policy-specific value.

9.6 “Best response” and “oracle ceiling” objective alignment

The baseline ceiling is a best response to a fixed opponent policy, while oracle ceiling is memoized expectimax after revealing hidden state. Ensure both optimize the same reward and evaluation distribution. If the baseline best response only has the player’s information state but the oracle sees full state, this is sensible; define it formally. If opponents are stochastic or chance histories matter, define the policy conditioning correctly.

9.7 Repeated cards and multiset counting

The correction for UNO and Mahjong is a good catch, but the paper should state how all duplicate-card games were audited. A reviewer may wonder whether other games also have equivalence/symmetry issues, including suit isomorphisms or identical action labels.

9.8 “Only one of 23” threshold statement

Ensure all 23 are comparable and that censored/unmeasured values are not being counted as low. If a game has only a lower bound at 6.32 due to saturation, it should not be confidently ordered below 30.1.

============================================================
10. SUGGESTED REVISED CLAIMS
============================================================

Current-style claim:
  “Gin Rummy is a genuinely information-rich game rather than a thin one.”

Better:
  “Under our information-set log-cardinality metric and sampling protocol, Gin Rummy has high observational ambiguity relative to the 2-player card configurations in this atlas.”

Current-style claim:
  “The hidden hand changes nothing.”

Better:
  “Appending the opponent’s hand yields no detectable improvement in win rate against the fixed reference under the evaluated learner and training protocol.”

Current-style claim:
  “The agent is learning-bound.”

Better:
  “The observed plateau is not relieved by direct opponent-hand revelation, so lack of this specific hidden information is not supported as the explanation for the plateau.”

Current-style claim:
  “Effort belongs in optimisation, reward and curriculum, not in belief modelling.”

Better:
  “These results prioritize optimization, reward, curriculum, and representation diagnostics; they do not rule out structured belief modeling or information-sensitive strategies in other evaluation settings.”

Current-style claim:
  “Resampling fails silently in both directions.”

Better:
  “Our sampling-based pipeline exhibits two silent failure modes: intrinsic right-censoring from finite sample support and a generator-degeneracy failure that repeatedly returns one compatible world.”

Current-style claim:
  “Exact enumeration is ground truth.”

Better:
  “Exact enumeration provides the exact log-cardinality for the implemented extensive-form game and its declared information-state representation.”

============================================================
11. PRIORITIZED REVISION PLAN
============================================================

Priority 0: Fix before anyone reads it

  1. Resolve the Table 2 numerical inconsistency (24.7 vs 25.5 versus 26.79 vs 27.04).
  2. Define exactly what “30.1 bits at a typical decision” means and how states are sampled/weighted.
  3. Add a formal statement distinguishing log-cardinality from entropy and value of information.
  4. Rephrase all claims that turn “no detectable oracle gain” into “information is worthless” or “belief modeling cannot help.”
  5. Clarify whether each atlas value is exact, proxy, right-censored lower bound, or unavailable.

Priority 1: High impact, modest effort

  6. Add a Gin Rummy worked counting example and an ambiguity-versus-game-stage plot/quantile table.
  7. Report oracle-minus-placebo with its own CI; state the exact statistical method and independent/paired design.
  8. Pre-specify or retrospectively but transparently state a practical effect threshold; add equivalence/power discussion.
  9. Rename/qualify the search measure as a confounded oracle-search gap.
  10. Rename “capacity probe” to “architecture sensitivity” unless there is a controlled capacity sweep.
  11. Add an explicit related-work/positioning paragraph.

Priority 2: Stronger paper if feasible

  12. Add one alternate frozen evaluation opponent.
  13. Add a Gin Rummy training-budget sensitivity check.
  14. Add an action-sensitivity or structured-oracle-feature diagnostic.
  15. Calibrate closed form against exact enumeration across every feasible row and report error distribution.
  16. Separate history count from current-latent-state count where possible.

Priority 3: Nice-to-have robustness

  17. Add posterior-entropy estimates in a small subset of games under a stated behavior policy to show divergence from log-cardinality.
  18. Provide a machine-readable atlas provenance table and exact scripts/versions.
  19. Add ablation of temporal persistence/canonical ordering for oracle/placebo channel.
  20. Add score-margin/per-hand return analyses alongside win rate.

============================================================
12. POTENTIAL REVIEWER QUESTIONS AND SUGGESTED RESPONSES
============================================================

Question: “Your 30.1 bits are not Shannon entropy. Why call them bits of hidden information?”

Response to prepare:
  “Correct: our primary metric is information-set log-cardinality, which we now call support bits/observational ambiguity. We use bits only as a logarithmic unit. We explicitly distinguish it from posterior entropy and decision value, both of which require a distribution and objective.”

Question: “What does ‘typical decision’ mean?”

Response to prepare:
  “It is an average/median over [exact state distribution]. We state the policy, weighting, player conditioning, and nonterminal-state handling. We also report Gin Rummy quantiles/phase plots.”

Question: “Could Gin Rummy’s null be underpowered?”

Response to prepare:
  “The 95% interval for the planned oracle-minus-baseline/plus oracle-minus-placebo contrast is [..]. We state the smallest practically important effect. We do not claim exact zero; we claim no detectable effect above the resolution supported by 12 seed-level training runs.”

Question: “Maybe raw opponent cards are hard to exploit, so your null is a learning failure, not low value.”

Response to prepare:
  “Yes; the raw oracle intervention identifies whether this learner recipe realizes a benefit, not the normative value of information. We avoid interpreting it as a proof of zero VOI. We add structured oracle-derived features/action-sensitivity analysis to distinguish representation/credit assignment from low action relevance.”

Question: “Why is your search gap an upper bound?”

Response to prepare:
  “We now call it a search-based oracle gap rather than a clean VOI bound. It is confounded by strategy fusion and planning differences. The exact ‘worth’ quantity is reserved for our solvable games.”

Question: “Why compare games using incompatible estimators?”

Response to prepare:
  “We do not claim all values have equal status. Each row shows estimator provenance: exact, combinatorial proxy, right-censored resampling lower bound, or unavailable. We use the mixed-method atlas primarily to expose measurement coverage/failure, while sensitivity analyses calibrate proxy error where exact values are feasible.”

Question: “Why call the rule-based player an expert?”

Response to prepare:
  “We use ‘fixed reference policy’ in the revised paper. The key property is that it is deterministic, frozen, cheap to evaluate, and observes a subset of the learner’s input—not that it establishes game-theoretic optimality.”

============================================================
13. SUGGESTED REVISED ABSTRACT (DRAFT)
============================================================

A win rate is only as informative as the reference policy and the information available to the learner. We study two quantities that are often conflated: observational ambiguity in a game and the cause of an agent’s performance plateau. First, across 88 configurations from OpenSpiel and RLCard, we measure information-set log-cardinality at sampled decision states: the log2 number of histories consistent with the acting player’s information state. This support-based quantity is not posterior entropy or the value of information, but it provides a provenance-aware map of what game observations leave unresolved. The atlas shows that two-player card configurations cluster at low values except for large-deal games such as Gin Rummy (30.1 support bits under our sampling protocol), that larger card-game values are largely driven by additional private hands, and that a sampling pipeline can fail silently through both sample-budget saturation and degenerate world generation. Second, we introduce controlled probes for a plateau against a frozen reference policy. In Gin Rummy, changing tested encoders does not improve performance, and appending the opponent’s true hand to the learner observation yields 26.79% win rate versus 27.04% for the baseline across 12 seeds (difference -0.25 percentage points; 95% interval [-1.78, +1.28]); a matched noninformative placebo channel yields 27.02%. Thus, in this setup, direct revelation of the opponent hand does not explain the observed plateau, despite high observational ambiguity. In solvable benchmarks, exact oracle and non-oracle ceilings separate the game-defined value of revelation from the fraction realized by a learned agent. Together, the results argue for reporting measurement provenance and for diagnosing hidden information, normative information value, and learnable use of information as distinct quantities.

============================================================
14. SUGGESTED NEW MAIN-TEXT PARAGRAPH ON DEFINITIONS
============================================================

Insert near the start of Part I:

“Throughout, our atlas reports information-set log-cardinality. For an acting player’s observation o, let I(o) denote the set of complete game histories compatible with that observation; our primary quantity is b_support(o)=log2|I(o)|. This is a support-size measure of observational ambiguity: it counts how many histories remain possible in the implemented game model. It is not posterior Shannon entropy, which would weight histories by a distribution induced by chance and policies, and it is not the decision-theoretic value of revealing the hidden state. Those distinctions matter below: a game may have many compatible hidden histories while revelation changes few optimal actions, and a small hidden variable may have high value when it flips a high-stakes decision.”

Then immediately state the sampling rule for “typical decision.”

============================================================
15. SUGGESTED NEW MAIN-TEXT PARAGRAPH ON THE GIN NULL
============================================================

Insert near the Gin oracle results:

“The oracle-observation result should not be read as evidence that the opponent hand has zero game-theoretic value. It identifies a narrower quantity: the improvement realized when this learner, trained with this recipe, receives a raw opponent-hand channel and is evaluated against this frozen reference policy. The confidence interval rules out only effects larger than its positive bound under the chosen analysis. The result nevertheless rules out two simpler explanations for the plateau: it is not explained by a generic cost of widening the input, because the matched placebo is near baseline, and the intervention is capable of detecting positive effects in our solvable control games. A remaining possibility is that the full hand contains action-relevant information that is difficult for the learner to transform into useful counterfactual features; we therefore distinguish realized oracle gain from the normative value of information.”

============================================================
16. FINAL VERDICT
============================================================

The manuscript has a compelling problem, strong experimental instincts, and an unusually good negative-result design. The place to improve is not by making the rhetoric louder. It is by making the estimands sharper.

The paper should explicitly separate:

  - what histories are compatible with an observation;
  - how probability mass is distributed across them;
  - how much an optimal decision-maker would gain from revelation;
  - how much this learned agent gains after raw revelation;
  - and how much apparent gain/loss is due to input formatting or differential optimization difficulty.

If revised around that hierarchy, the Gin Rummy result becomes more, not less, interesting. It stops being a puzzling claim that “30 hidden bits are worthless” and becomes a disciplined empirical demonstration that high observational ambiguity need not translate into a detectable improvement from a raw oracle channel in a particular agent–opponent–training system.

That distinction is a meaningful contribution to trustworthy RL evaluation and imperfect-information game benchmarking.
